comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text: This is also certainly a contributing factor to the anomalous temperature readings we were getting on these boxes. (We took this box apart a few weeks ago to investigate the thermistors).

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Diagnosis on Preheim voltage drop issue:

Box 2 (590 D4) pulled.
Tested our cheap miliohmeter on the MEB_S3 and misc. busbars.
The tool: I'm not 100% convinced on the absolute values, which seem higher than should be expected even in a 'perfect' scenario... I think we can chalk that up to the quality of the leads. This Amazon special is like $130 total... Hioki leads by themselves are $250-$750.The tool itself is solid. Consistent, reliable readings, maintains it's 'zero' point, you can re-test the same connection after testing a few others and the value is accurate to the uOhm. So these values are useful compared to themselves, not to what we actually expect if we were measuring with a $2000 meter.

What I found is that there was a lack of contact at all three of the 'lateral' busbars (going from side-to-side on a module).

You can see this in the NOOXID pattern on the busbars. The module connections which had the worst values had the smallest area of NOOXID compression.

This is primarily due to insufficient material cut out of the protective housing on the 590s.  This caused the plastic to be .5mm-1.5mm proud of the terminal, causing the busbar to not make full contact. You could also see a small amount of plastic being smashed between the busbar and the terminal.

A secondary cause was excessive insulation on the busbars, which interfered with the plastic housing.

It wasn't pretty, but I was able to trim down the excess plastic using fine snips to where no further material was proud. I also trimmed back the insulation where necessary. This would be much more easily accomplished prior to installation.

Measurements were taken from internal-module-busbar directly adjacent to the desired joint to be measured. Meter was zerod to this value to reduce discrepancies relating to mating surface.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Troubleshoot voltage issue — work performed August 10, 2026
I set up the Vici VC480C+ micro-ohmmeter on the 20 mΩ range and verified its zero behavior by re-zeroing on a terminal-to-terminal placement and re-measuring each joint. Implied offset was 0.69 / 0.73 / 0.68 mΩ across spans of 1.19–1.92 mΩ, with no relationship to reading magnitude. Repeatability is ±0.025 mΩ. All readings below are terminal-zeroed.
I measured all three module-to-module busbar joints in Box 2 over two passes. As found: 1-to-2 at 1.23 mΩ, 2-to-3 at 0.46 mΩ, 3-to-4 at 0.72 mΩ. Ranking held across both passes.
I pulled the 1-to-2 and 3-to-4 busbars. The NO-OX-ID witness pattern showed partial compression on both. The orange terminal housing on the LYTH VDA590 sits up to 1.7 mm proud of the terminal face and was visibly crushed between busbar and terminal.
I trimmed the housing, applied NO-OX-ID and reinstalled each joint. On 3-to-4 I also found HV insulation fouling the joint face and removed it. 2-to-3 needed the housing cut down but no insulation trim.
Results

undefined
3-to-4 read 0.56 mΩ reinstalled dry, before insulation removal and NO-OX-ID.
Documented with 72 photos.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
TLDR: Anyone building 590s be very sure that these plastic housings are cut well below the face of the terminal.

We will need to pull the other two boxes to rectify. The other D4 will be a similar procedure to this box. The D8 will need to be disassembled to the point we can access the inner busbars.

comments.author: David Webber
comments.text:
Car is back on the ground and sitting at or close to a proper ride height. If anything, the front of the car may be just slightly high. Spacing the spring pan down with spacers or washers should correct this.

The factory-specified overall height for a 1962 Jaguar Mark 2 (MK2) is 57.5 inches (146.1 cm) at kerb weight. The standard ground clearance is exactly 7 inches (17.8 cm). [1, 2, 3]
Because the vehicle uses coil springs in the front and semi-elliptical leaf springs in the back, checking the physical ride height is often done using specific points: [1, 2, 3, 4]
Front: The correct front suspension height is achieved when the lower wishbone arms are perfectly parallel/level with the front subframe. Enthusiast consensus suggests that you should be able to fit about "three fingers" vertically between the front tire and the top of the wheel arch.
Rear: The general enthusiast consensus suggests a measurement of 18.5 to 19 inches from the ground up to the center of the boot lock. [1, 2, 3]
How to Adjust the Ride Height
Front: Front ride height is set by coil springs. If it is too high (common after installing new, modern replacement springs), owners typically use shims or washers placed between the lower control arm and the spring pan to achieve the desired drop. [1, 2, 3]
Rear: The rear height is dictated by leaf springs. Adjustments to the rear require adding or removing spacers/shims between the rear axle and the leaf springs. [1, 2, 3]

I will re-evaluate this once car has been driven

comments.author: David Webber
comments.text: MR2 power steering pump can be heard to run but it doesn't feel as if it provides any assist. Installed a pressure gauge inline with the pressure leg, down stream of the pressure regulator. This gauge reads zero pressure regardless of steering input or regulator adjustment. Installed replacement pump & the pressure gauge now displays a max of 300psi with steering input & regulator adjustment doesn't seem to have an effect of pressure. Steering feels a little heavy but doesn't feel unassisted. Moved the pressure gauge to take a reading of the pump before the regulator and the gauge still displays a maximum pressure of 300psi. The next step will be to remove the regulator altogether to see how the system behaves, and decide on how to proceed based on this information.

comments.text: Worked with Brandon to develop a better PMU revision system. Cleaned up the master branch and backed up on google drive. Had Brandon pull this down and showed him how to flash to the PMU's along with a number of other vehicle startup details to follow along first. Moved on to the VCU, showed Brandon about the firmware builds and Raptor structures. Converted vehicle requirements into a VCU config. Moved on to the inverter while Brandon loaded that. comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued startup with Brandon and Dave. Hooked up HV and key'd on. Tried charging and got the ChgPortContFlt, verified all the associated wiring that has caused that fault previously, no problems found. Tried charging again and it just worked this time. Verified battery heater. Calibrated the resolver. Troubleshot cabin heater wiring. Searched and searched for documentation but couldn't find complete references. Experementially found the VCU was telling the PMU to tell the VCU to turn on the heat. Took thorough notes on actual wiring.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified K33 "Heat Request" functionality on Prehiem to make sure I had the correct tags in Raptor-Service. Tried various combinations of PMU outputs and VCU configs to determine if there was a way to get powering up the heater logic unit as the mechanism to enable heat. Ends up with a fault in the VCU which makes adding a relay the easier option. Drew a diagram for and wired up a relay to a spare output on the PMU. Wrote logic to check the temp knob below 15%, the fan knob above 30%, as well as negative contactor and ignition on. Tested all knob positions and GUI inputs while watching in Raptor and the PMU software. The GUI indicates correctly and warm air blows. I never let it heat up enough to judge effectiveness. Only thing left for HVAC now is to charge the AC and tune that in.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified heater circuit actually working by monitoring CAN data from the heater itself for output power. Double checked with a second data source Pack_Current from the BMS. Modified the PMU logic to also include fan and temp knobs as a criteria for turning on the cabin heat pump. Tested all scenarious with the user inputs from the GUI and knobs. Noticed the battery pump was running when it usually isn't, started to investigate, met for various discussions with the team before I could finish. Plugged into Preheim to investigate source of the difference in control.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Tuned in the AC compressor with Dave, it's working as expected plus a little 'bonus'. The AC compressor 'hiccups' with HV connected but the logic unit powered off. Powering up the compressor logic controller without Ampere commanding it to actually compress causes a VCU level fault. Shared to Slack.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Catching up on Slack before the meeting. Looked into Claudes diagnosis of the AC issue. Looks like the PMU program has never changed for that channel and Claude picked up on the troubleshooting I did as the actual problem, not knowing that at time the system was supposed to be operating different than the rest of the fleet. This was required to verify the 450V compressor functions differently than the 400V one and would work better under a different control sequence. Verified VCU settings for the battery were wrong and corrected.

The new battery health calculations result in 146.4 Ah for the pack, a very reasonable estimate. Also verified Dave's findings on the AC compressor from the computer side. The hiccup issue has been magically fixed.
